bisexuality is a silenced sexuality in South Africa and that this is a result of the interplay between race, class, gender, space and sexuality.
bisexual erasure is a complex phenomenon that occurs through a variety of acts of non-recogntion and misrecognition and that it is possible for women to resist these acts.
bisexuality is a “silenced sexuality” both in the South African context and in the academic literature.
In summary, our research is concerned with
bisexual identity as an embodied and lived experience.
the ways that bisexual erasure operates in South African society, the effects of this erasure and the possibilities for resistance to the erasure.
the lived experiences of bisexual women, their everyday struggles, and how they negotiate their identities.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the bisexual female identity is not a legitimate sexual identity in South Africa, and that it is not possible to live as a “self-aware bisexual female identity” without experiencing erasure.
bisexual women are erased through the denial of their identity as women.
the bisexual identity is a silenced one, and that the silencing occurs through a variety of means, but is most often the result of a failure to recognise the bisexual identity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
bisexuality is a “suspended sexuality” in South Africa, and that this suspension is not evenly distributed.
bisexual erasure is not a single event, nor is it a singular phenomenon.
bisexual identity is a “complex and contradictory” identity, one that is often erased, but that also provides a space for resistance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
bisexuality is not a “choice”, it is a way of being in the world that has been shaped by a history of oppression and resistance.
bisexual erasure is an everyday occurrence, and that bisexuals are not passive victims of erasure but are active agents in resisting it.
the experiences of black bisexual women in the context of the South African post-apartheid moment are complex and multifaceted and cannot be reduced to a single narrative of oppression.
